title: Discriminated unions and tagged unions
hook: When each variant of a union carries a shared tag field like `kind` or `type`, TypeScript can follow that tag and unlock the right fields automatically — the pattern behind most well-typed API responses and state machines.

blocks.text: A **discriminated union** (also called a **tagged union**) is a union of object types that share a common **discriminant** property — usually a string literal field like `kind`, `type`, or `status`. When you compare that field, TypeScript **narrows** the whole object to the matching variant. Combined with **`never`-based exhaustiveness**, adding a new variant forces compiler errors in every `switch`. C# achieves similar ergonomics with **pattern matching** on records and `switch` expressions; TypeScript does it with structural unions and flow analysis.

entries.plainDefinition: A shared literal-typed field on every union member that identifies which variant you hold.
entries.example: `{ kind: "circle"; radius: number } | { kind: "square"; side: number }`

entries.plainDefinition: Another name for discriminated union — the tag tells the compiler which shape is active.
A switch over the discriminant where the default branch assigns to never, proving all variants handled.
entries.example: See union-types topic for the never pattern.

blocks.text: Plain unions of unrelated shapes (`string | number`) need typeof guards. Object unions without a discriminant require **`in` checks** on every branch. A discriminant gives you one reliable switch point — the standard pattern for **Result/Either** types, HTTP response modeling, form wizard steps, and finite state machines. It is the single most important TypeScript pattern for replacing `any` in business logic.

blocks.title: Discriminant must be a literal
blocks.body: The tag field must be typed as a string literal (or boolean/number literal), not plain `string`. If `kind: string`, comparing `kind === "circle"` does not narrow — use `kind: "circle"` on that member.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Define each variant
items.body: Each member is an object type with the same discriminant key and a unique literal value.

items.title: Union the variants
items.body: `type Shape = Circle | Square | Triangle` — one parameter type for all shapes.

items.title: Switch on the discriminant
items.body: `switch (shape.kind)` — each case narrows to one variant.

items.title: Prove exhaustiveness
items.body: Default branch with `never` — compiler enforces updates when variants grow.

diagram.title: Discriminated union narrowing
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  U["Shape union"] --> SW{"switch kind"}
  SW -->|circle| C["radius available"]
  SW -->|square| S["side available"]
  SW -->|triangle| T["base + height"]
  SW -->|default| N["never — missing case?"]

snippet.label: Classic shape discriminated union
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: shared `kind` literal distinguishes variants. Line 7: switching on `kind` narrows `shape`. Lines 8–9: `radius` only exists on Circle — legal after narrowing. Lines 11–14: exhaustiveness guard for future variants.

snippet.label: API Result type — success or failure
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: boolean discriminant `ok` separates success and failure. Line 6: `!result.ok` narrows to `ApiFailure` in the if-block. Line 9: after the throw, `result` is `ApiSuccess<T>` — `data` is safe.

snippet.label: Redux-style action union
snippet.explanation: Line 3: `type` field is the discriminant — conventional in Redux. Lines 7–10: each case sees the correct payload fields. This pattern scales to dozens of actions with exhaustiveness checking.

snippet.label: Failure mode — non-literal discriminant
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: `kind: string` prevents narrowing — both members allow any string. Line 7: comparison to a literal does not refine the union when the discriminant is not a literal type. Always use unique literal values per variant.

rows: Records / discriminated unions in F#-style C#

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `string` instead of a literal for the discriminant. Forgetting exhaustiveness when the union grows. Mixing variants that use different discriminant key names (`kind` vs `type`) in the same union.

blocks.text: Discriminated unions are the TypeScript answer to **algebraic data types (ADTs)**. Pair with `satisfies` operator to validate object literals while preserving literal types. For JSON APIs, validate discriminant at runtime (Zod, io-ts) then narrow — compile-time tags do not survive untrusted input. **Discriminated unions + mapped types** power reducer typing in advanced libraries. C# 11+ `switch` on records is the closest idiomatic comparison for interview cross-talk.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Verbose, easy to miss a branch

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain why literal discriminant is required. No exhaustiveness strategy. Comparing to C# enums only — enums are nominal and lack per-variant payloads unless attributed.

interviewTakeaways: Discriminated unions share a literal tag field — kind, type, or status.
Switching on the tag narrows the whole object to one variant.
Combine with never in default for compile-time exhaustiveness.
The discriminant must be a literal type, not plain string.
60s: Tagged union = shared literal field + variant payloads. Switch narrows. never catches missing cases. C# uses record patterns; TS uses structural unions.
commonPitfalls: kind: string instead of kind: "circle" — narrowing fails.
No exhaustiveness check when the union grows in a large codebase.
Strong answer: 'Literal tag narrows the union. never proves exhaustiveness. Validate JSON at runtime before trusting the tag.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Redux actions and AST nodes use `type` fields at runtime. TypeScript adds compile-time narrowing on top of the same JS object shape.
C# `result switch { Success s => ..., Failure f => ... }` mirrors TS discriminated unions. C# is nominal; TS is structural.
